(CNN) -- Former Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Vick left a federal prison in Leavenworth, Kansas, early Wednesday, according to his publicist and the Federal Bureau of Prisons. Michael Vick, left, arrives at federal court with attorney Billy Martin in Richmond, Viriginia, in 2007. He will serve the last two months of his 23-month sentence in home confinement in Virginia, his publicist Judy Smith said. He is a native of Newport News, Virginia. Vick, 28, pleaded guilty in August 2007 to a federal charge of bankrolling a dogfighting operation at a home he owned in Virginia. He will return to professional football as soon as September if reinstated by the NFL, according to the sports agent who negotiated Vick's 10-year, $140 million contract with the Falcons. Meanwhile, Vick's attorneys have said he will work at a Newport News construction firm following his release, and he has also agreed to participate in a documentary for $600,000. Last month, a federal bankruptcy judge denied a Chapter 11 bankruptcy plan presented by Vick, urging him to offer the court another plan to emerge from bankruptcy. The plan called for Vick to come up with $750,000 to $1 million in cash to be paid to creditors, U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Frank Santoro said, but added he saw no evidence Vick could come up with that much. Santoro suggested Vick's next plan not call for him to keep two houses and three cars, as did the rejected proposal. In testimony, Vick acknowledged committing a "heinous" act and said he should have acted more maturely. He said he has been earning 12 cents an hour as an overnight janitor in prison. His Falcons salary, he said, was between $10 million and $12 million. He acknowledged failing to handle his money well.  Watch a panel discuss his release » . Vick plans to work with the Humane Society of the United States on anti-dogfighting campaigns, Humane Society President Wayne Pacelle told CNN on Tuesday. Vick will work on programs aimed at preventing youths from getting involved in dogfighting, and also on programs to assist young people who have already been involved in the blood sport. Pacelle said the Humane Society was approached by Vick's representatives. He said he has traveled to Kansas twice to meet with the former quarterback, and during the second visit, the two discussed how Vick could use his sway over youths to discourage them from involvement in dogfighting, as well as help those who were apprehended in connection with it.  Watch more about Vick's dogs » . Details have not yet been hammered out, Pacelle said, but will be in the next couple of days. iReport.com: Does Vick deserve a second chance? More attention has been paid to dogfighting as a result of Vick's case, Pacelle said. The Humane Society, which offers rewards for tips involving dogfighting, has recently paid out $40,000 in five different cases, he said.

(CNN) — Michael Vick, the former Atlanta Falcons quarterback, was released from the federal prison in Leavenworth, Kansas, early Wednesday, his publicist and the Federal Bureau of Prisons reported.

Vick, who was photographed arriving at federal court in Richmond, Virginia, with attorney Billy Martin in 2007, will complete the final two months of his 23-month sentence under home confinement in Virginia, according to publicist Judy Smith. The 28-year-old is originally from Newport News, Virginia.

In August 2007, Vick admitted guilt to a federal charge involving the financing of a dogfighting enterprise operated from a Virginia property he owned.

The agent who negotiated Vick’s 10-year, $140 million Falcons contract said the quarterback could return to professional football as early as September, provided the NFL reinstates him. His lawyers have also said that, after leaving prison, Vick will take a job with a construction company in Newport News. In addition, he has accepted a $600,000 deal to appear in a documentary.

A federal bankruptcy judge rejected Vick’s proposed Chapter 11 reorganization plan last month and instructed him to submit a different strategy for exiting bankruptcy. U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Frank Santoro said the proposal required Vick to provide between $750,000 and $1 million in cash for creditors, but the judge found no proof that Vick could raise that amount. Santoro also recommended that the next proposal not allow Vick to retain two homes and three vehicles, as the denied plan had.

During his testimony, Vick described his conduct as “heinous,” said he should have demonstrated greater maturity, and conceded that he had managed his finances poorly. He reported earning 12 cents per hour while working nights as a prison janitor, compared with an annual Falcons salary of between $10 million and $12 million. A panel discussed his release.

Humane Society of the United States President Wayne Pacelle told CNN on Tuesday that Vick intends to join the organization’s efforts against dogfighting. His work will include initiatives designed both to keep young people from entering dogfighting and to help youths who have already participated in the blood sport.

According to Pacelle, Vick’s representatives initiated contact with the Humane Society. Pacelle said he made two trips to Kansas to meet the former quarterback. During their second meeting, they considered ways Vick could use his influence with young people to deter them from dogfighting and support those arrested in connection with the activity. Additional coverage addressed Vick’s dogs.

Although the arrangement had not yet been finalized, Pacelle said the remaining details were expected to be settled within the next several days.

An iReport.com prompt asked whether Vick deserved another opportunity. Pacelle said Vick’s prosecution had brought increased public attention to dogfighting. He added that the Humane Society, which pays rewards for information about such activity, had recently distributed a total of $40,000 in connection with five separate cases.

**HAMPTON, Virginia (CNN) —** Former NFL quarterback Michael Vick left a federal prison in Kansas on Wednesday and returned to Virginia, where he will serve the final two months of his sentence in home confinement.

Vick, once one of professional football’s highest-profile players, was released from the federal penitentiary in Leavenworth after serving most of a 23-month sentence for his role in a dogfighting operation.

He arrived at his home in Hampton, Virginia, early Wednesday, according to his attorneys. Under the terms of his confinement, Vick will be monitored electronically and allowed to leave the residence only for approved activities, including work and meetings with federal officials.

Vick pleaded guilty in 2007 to a federal conspiracy charge after admitting that he helped operate “Bad Newz Kennels,” a dogfighting venture based on property he owned in Surry County, Virginia. Court documents said dogs that performed poorly were killed by drowning, hanging and other methods.

The case ended Vick’s career with the Atlanta Falcons and prompted the NFL to suspend him indefinitely. The Falcons later released him.

Vick is expected to work in a construction-related job while in home confinement. His federal sentence is scheduled to end in July, after which he will remain under supervised release.

His possible return to the NFL remains uncertain. Commissioner Roger Goodell has said he would review Vick’s status after the quarterback completed his sentence and demonstrated remorse.

Vick, a former No. 1 overall draft pick known for his speed and powerful arm, has said he hopes to rebuild his life and resume his football career. Animal welfare groups, however, have argued that any decision about reinstatement should reflect the severity of the crimes.

No immediate decision on his NFL future was expected.

## Michael Vick leaves Leavenworth prison, begins home confinement after dogfighting sentence

**HAMPTON, Va., May 20, 2009** — Former Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Vick was released from the federal penitentiary in Leavenworth, Kansas, early Wednesday after serving most of a 23-month sentence for his role in an interstate dogfighting operation.

Vick, once one of the National Football League’s highest-paid and most recognizable players, was expected to return to Virginia to serve the final portion of his sentence in home confinement. His movement will remain restricted, and he will be monitored by federal authorities before his sentence formally ends in July.

The release marks the start of a difficult attempt at personal, financial and professional rehabilitation for the former No. 1 overall draft pick, whose football career collapsed after investigators uncovered the dogfighting enterprise known as **Bad Newz Kennels** at property he owned in Surry County, Virginia.

### Dogfighting conviction

Vick pleaded guilty in federal court in 2007 to conspiring to operate an interstate dogfighting venture and to related gambling activity. Prosecutors said Vick and his associates financed and managed fights, traveled across state lines and killed dogs that performed poorly.

Court filings described especially brutal methods used to kill some animals, including hanging and drowning. Vick acknowledged participating in the destruction of dogs and admitted that he had helped fund the operation.

U.S. District Judge Henry E. Hudson sentenced Vick to 23 months in prison, a term longer than prosecutors had initially recommended. The judge questioned Vick’s candor and conduct after the investigation began, including a failed drug test while he was awaiting sentencing.

Vick later entered a guilty plea to state dogfighting charges in Virginia and received a suspended sentence, avoiding additional time behind bars after completion of his federal punishment.

Many of the dogs seized from the property were placed with rescue groups. After behavioral evaluations, a number were rehabilitated and adopted, challenging the assumption that animals taken from fighting operations must automatically be euthanized.

### Career and finances collapse

Before the scandal, Vick had signed a 10-year, $130 million contract with the Falcons and had earned millions more through endorsements. His speed, powerful arm and improvisational style made him one of the league’s biggest attractions.

The conviction brought that success to an abrupt end. The NFL suspended him indefinitely, the Falcons moved on without him, and corporate sponsors ended endorsement relationships.

Vick also faced extensive financial problems. He filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 2008, reporting millions of dollars in debts to banks, former business partners, agents and other creditors. The Falcons sought to recover a substantial portion of the signing bonuses paid under his contract, while legal fees, declining assets and questionable investments added to his difficulties.

Under a court-supervised bankruptcy plan, Vick was expected to devote much of his future income to repaying creditors. His finances remained under close scrutiny, and any return to professional football would have significant consequences for the repayment process.

### Construction work during home confinement

As part of his transition from prison, Vick arranged to work at a construction-related job in Virginia. Reports said he would earn about **$10 an hour**, a dramatic contrast with the salary he received as an NFL quarterback.

The job was intended to satisfy federal requirements that he maintain approved employment while in home confinement. He was expected to be allowed to leave his residence only for work and other activities authorized by corrections officials.

Vick also remained subject to probation conditions and financial obligations, including restrictions imposed through his bankruptcy case.

### Rehabilitation and animal-welfare work

Vick’s representatives said he hoped to demonstrate remorse and rebuild public trust. He agreed to work with the **Humane Society of the United States** on programs intended to discourage young people from becoming involved in dogfighting.

The proposed outreach was expected to include appearances at schools and community events, particularly in urban areas where organized dogfighting has persisted. Humane Society officials said Vick’s participation could be useful if he spoke honestly about the cruelty involved and the consequences of his conduct.

The partnership was controversial. Some animal advocates argued that Vick should not quickly be treated as a spokesman for animal welfare and questioned whether his remorse was genuine. Others said his notoriety could help reach audiences that traditional anti-dogfighting campaigns had struggled to influence.

Vick also indicated that he would seek counseling and continue efforts to understand the harm caused by the operation. His rehabilitation campaign was expected to be judged not by a single apology or appearance, but by sustained conduct over time.

### NFL future uncertain

Vick’s release does not automatically restore his eligibility to play professional football. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, who suspended Vick indefinitely in 2007, has said he would evaluate whether Vick had accepted responsibility and shown genuine remorse before deciding on reinstatement.

Even if reinstated, Vick would still need a team willing to sign him and withstand the public reaction. After nearly two full seasons away from the game, questions also remain about his conditioning and ability to return to an NFL offense.

For now, Vick’s immediate priorities are completing home confinement, complying with bankruptcy and probation requirements, maintaining employment and beginning his promised anti-dogfighting work.

His departure from Leavenworth closes the prison phase of the case, but it does not end the legal, financial and reputational consequences of a scandal that transformed him from an NFL superstar into one of the most controversial figures in American sports.
